headline: A US diesel export ban would shock global seaborne markets — US supplies ~25% of global seaborne diesel and ~90% of Latin America's seaborne diesel imports
reasoning: The US currently accounts for about 25% of global seaborne diesel supply, running at approximately 1.6 million barrels per day in August, a near all-time high. Roughly 90% of Latin America's seaborne diesel imports originate from the US, and about 25% of Europe's seaborne diesel imports also come from the US. A 90-day export ban would provide short-term domestic price relief along the Gulf Coast, Midwest and East Coast, but would significantly disrupt global seaborne markets. Over a prolonged period, the ban would reduce refinery utilisation and eventually push domestic diesel prices higher again.

Also keep in mind, roughly 90% of Latin America's seaborne imports of diesel come from the United States. And so that that's a critical, um, trade flow pattern that would be impacted even into Europe. Roughly 25% of Europe's seaborne imports of diesel come from the United States. So again, in the international market, it would be a shock. Domestically, the immediate impact. You'd likely see lower diesel prices along the Gulf Coast in the Midwest, and likely on the East Coast as well. However, if you were to keep some kind of export ban in place over a long period of time, you would definitely see impacts to refinery utilization.

headline: Global wheat supply through peak harvest season to fall ~30% due to Russia-Ukraine conflict; Egypt, Tunisia and other import-dependent developing economies most exposed

Rich developed economies like Europe will absorb higher prices, but import-dependent economies in North Africa and the Middle East — with limited fiscal and monetary buffers — face severe food security risk if grain availability problems persist, which he expects they will.
